title: Evaluating a Generate–Validate–Repair Pipeline for LLM‑based Network Configuration: a Paired, Emulation‑Grounded Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired, emulation‑grounded experiment (N=240 paired intents) to test whether integrating a deterministic network verifier into a generate–validate–repair (GVR) pipeline reduces unsafe configuration applications from an LLM compared with an LLM‑only pipeline. Tasks were drawn as 60% in‑distribution, 20% distribution‑shift, and 20% adversarial‑prompt, and the experiment used shared_initial_candidate semantics (one initial LLM generation per task reused across paired arms). The guarded arm could invoke up to one validator‑triggered repair. All 240 paired tasks were scored safe under both arms, yielding a paired difference = 0.00 (95% bootstrap CI [0.00,0.00]; exact McNemar p = 1.0). Deterministic reconciliation shows no repair was invoked because every shared initial generation passed the deterministic validator. We report the preregistered design, complete execution and analysis artifacts, an explicit statement of sampling metadata (temperature recorded as null/unset and per-call traces archived), an interpretation of the null outcome under shared_initial_candidate semantics, and concrete recommendations for future emulation‑grounded NetOps evaluations.

sections.introduction: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed to translate high‑level operator intent into concrete device configurations and to assist NetOps workflows. Prior emulation‑grounded evaluations show that closed‑loop testing can surface planning and execution failures that static text metrics miss [1]. A common mitigation pattern is generate–validate–repair (GVR): LLM generation followed by deterministic validation and iterative repair [2,3]. We preregistered a confirmatory, paired experiment to test whether inserting a deterministic verifier into an LLM pipeline reduces the rate of unsafe configuration applications in an emulation‑grounded benchmark. Our contributions are: (1) a preregistered paired study executed on a NetConfArena‑style emulator (study id study‑cand‑1‑gvr‑verifier‑adversarial‑2026‑08‑01); (2) full archival of execution, per‑call traces, and analysis artifacts; and (3) a failure‑analytic interpretation of a null outcome and actionable design recommendations for future NetOps evaluations.
sections.related_work: Executable NetOps benchmarks that run LLM agents in closed‑loop emulators have appeared recently to reveal workflow and planning faults beyond syntax [1]. Research on automated configuration repair and program repair documents generate‑and‑validate patterns and shows practical gains in constrained settings [2,4]. Survey and position works emphasize tool augmentation, verifier gating, and uncertainty calibration as architectural components to improve safety and operator trust, while noting gaps in domain‑specific calibration and integrated verifier evaluation at scale [3,5]. Our study builds directly on these lines by implementing a preregistered, paired GVR vs LLM‑only comparison under execution‑grounded scoring.
sections.methodology: Design and preregistration: We preregistered a paired binary design (registered plan id study‑cand‑1‑gvr‑verifier‑adversarial‑2026‑08‑01) comparing (A) baseline LLM‑only and (B) guarded GVR (deterministic_netops_validator_v5 plus up to one repair). The experiment used shared_initial_candidate semantics: a single initial generation per task was produced and reused across paired episodes; only validator‑triggered repair could produce paired divergences. Primary estimand: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline (absolute paired difference in unsafe‑apply rate). Sampling and power: N=240 paired tasks blocked into topology/vendor clusters; in‑distribution 60% (144), distribution‑shift 20% (48), adversarial‑prompt 20% (48). The preregistered power plan targeted detecting an absolute reduction of 8 percentage points with alpha = 0.05 and N=240 pairs. Model and execution: a single hosted model (declared_model_version = "gpt-5-mini") produced one shared initial candidate per task; the guarded adapter invoked deterministic_netops_validator_v5 and could issue at most one repair call per task. All model calls, per‑call sampling metadata, provider traces, and validator traces were archived. Sampling metadata and determinism: execution/model_configuration.json (path: execution/model_configuration.json; SHA‑256: a40e96e212ab87da251ac0d6dbb75bc543afa13438b5a6b9ebd073597ffdd820) records declared_model_version="gpt-5-mini" and temperature = null (unset). Null/unset does not imply deterministic sampling; per‑call sampling and seed traces are archived under execution/provider_calls/ (representative file execution/provider_calls/task-000004-shared-initial.json, SHA‑256: c17c77a79ac973a1c931bf5882e59bfa0039e53bac00ddc2cfc7d686ccb70467). Execution contract: the adapter used hosted_model calls limited by the preregistered maximum; planned_episode_count = 480 (240 pairs × shared_initial semantics), and completed_episode_count = 480. Scoring and outcome: the emulator deterministically executed final configurations and scored each episode as unsafe_apply (1) or safe_apply (0) according to the preregistered deterministic validation and simulator checks. Analysis: primary analysis used the registered paired_binary_analysis_v1 executor with paired bootstrap percentile CIs and an exact McNemar two‑sided test; bootstrap resamples = 10,000, seed = 1729. exclusion and missingness rules followed the preregistration (see archived preregistration SHA‑256: 3e73ca0d...).
sections.results: Execution and primary outcome: The run completed per the preregistered manifest: 240 paired tasks, 480 episodes, and 240 shared initial model calls. Every paired episode was scored safe under both arms: baseline_success_rate = 1.0 (240/240), guarded_success_rate = 1.0 (240/240). Contingency counts: n11 = 240, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. Estimated paired difference = 0.00; paired bootstrap 95% CI = [0.00, 0.00]; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0 (bootstrap resamples = 10,000; seed = 1729). Repair activity and model calls: no validator‑triggered repair was applied in any guarded episode (repair_attempts = 0 for all guarded episodes), and total hosted model calls used = 240 (one shared initial call per task), consistent with the shared_initial_candidate preregistration. Deterministic reconciliation and accounting: the archived deterministic_reconciliation.json confirms completed_episode_count = 480, complete_pair_count = 240, baseline_success_count = 240, guarded_success_count = 240, and provider_call_audit showing hosted_model_call_event_count = 240 and stage_counts {shared_initial_generation: 240}. Statistical consequence of observed contingency: because n10 = n01 = 0 (no discordant pairs), the preregistered primary paired test is uninformative for detecting a reduction in unsafe applies in this execution—there were no observed unsafe baseline applications to reduce. The observed bounds in archived analysis outputs are exact: point estimate 0.00 and 95% bootstrap CI [0.00,0.00], so the experiment provides a demonstrable null result under the preregistered estimand and the adopted shared_initial_candidate semantics. Relation to preregistered power plan: the preregistered power calculation targeted detecting an 8 percentage‑point absolute reduction starting from an assumed nonzero baseline unsafe rate; with observed baseline unsafe rate = 0 the planned detectable effect is not applicable (no positive reduction is possible), and thus statistical power to demonstrate a positive reduction is vacuous for these data.
sections.discussion: Interpretation: The confirmatory hypothesis (that GVR reduces unsafe applications) is not supported in this execution, but this null outcome is informative given the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics. The deterministic verifier cannot change the paired outcome unless the single shared initial candidate fails validation; because every initial candidate passed the validator, no repair opportunities arose and the guarded arm had no effect. Experimental‑design lesson: under shared_initial_candidate semantics a verifier can only demonstrate benefit if (i) the task generator or sampling semantics produce some verifier‑failing initial candidates, (ii) adversarial probes reliably induce validator failures, or (iii) the design permits independent initial draws per arm or larger repair budgets. Practical recommendations: future emulation‑grounded NetOps evaluations aiming to measure verifier benefit should (a) include independent generation per arm or increase repair budget, (b) strengthen adversary generation (adaptive adversaries beyond the preregistered fixed attacker seed), and (c) vary verifier coverage (add semantic checks in addition to syntactic/workflow checks) and measure verifier false‑safe rates by cross‑comparing verifier PASS with independent simulator outcomes. Threats to validity: internal validity is constrained by the shared_initial_candidate preregistration and single‑model scope; construct validity by the finite coverage of deterministic_netops_validator_v5; external validity by the emulation corpus (NetConfArena‑style synthetic device images and parameterized tasks) and single‑model testing; conclusion validity is limited because observed baseline unsafe rate = 0 makes the primary hypothesis inherently untestable in this run. We archived representative task, response, provider trace, and validator trace artifacts (examples in execution/ and analysis/), and all analysis artifacts are available in the execution bundle to support reanalysis and alternative experimental semantics.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered, paired, emulation‑grounded evaluation of a generate–validate–repair pipeline for LLM‑based network configuration. Observed outcomes were safe in every paired episode under both LLM‑only and GVR arms, producing an exact paired difference of 0.00 (95% bootstrap CI [0.00,0.00]; McNemar p = 1.0). Deterministic reconciliation shows that the guarded pipeline never invoked repairs because the single shared initial generation passed the deterministic validator for every task. This null result highlights an important experimental-design point: under shared_initial_candidate semantics only validator‑failing initial candidates can enable the verifier to alter paired outcomes. We provide the preregistration, execution manifest, per‑call traces, and analysis artifacts to support follow‑up tests that vary generation semantics, adversary strength, and verifier coverage. References: [1] C. Liu et al., "NetConfArena: An Executable Benchmark for LLM Agents in Closed‑Loop Network Configuration," arXiv, 2026. [2] Z. Gu et al., "Astragalus: Automatic Configuration Repair for Production Networks," arXiv, 2026. [3] M. Bilal et al., "Large Language Models for Agentic NetOps and AIOps: Architectures, Evaluation, and Safety," arXiv, 2026. [4] A. Yehudai et al., "A Survey on Evaluation of LLM‑based Agents," Findings ACL, 2026. [5] M. Xiong et al., "Can LLMs Express Their Uncertainty? An Empirical Evaluation of Confidence Elicitation in LLMs," arXiv, 2023.

disclosure_statement: Models and prompts: The study used a single hosted model (declared_model_version = "gpt-5-mini") called by the registered adapter 'hosted_netops_gvr_v1'. The exact immutable initial master prompt is archived at provenance/master_prompt.txt (SHA‑256: 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba). Model configuration and sampling metadata: execution/model_configuration.json (path: execution/model_configuration.json; SHA‑256: a40e96e212ab87da251ac0d6dbb75bc543afa13438b5a6b9ebd073597ffdd820) records temperature = null (unset) in the recorded model configuration. Null/unset does not imply deterministic sampling; per‑call sampling parameters and provider traces are archived under execution/provider_calls/ (representative file execution/provider_calls/task-000004-shared-initial.json; SHA‑256: c17c77a79ac973a1c931bf5882e59bfa0039e53bac00ddc2cfc7d686ccb70467). Human role and autonomy: a human Research Director selected the broad topic family (Generative AI / LLMs for NetOps) and constrained the initial master prompt prior to the autonomy lock. After the autonomy lock the pipeline autonomously performed literature selection, preregistration, experiment design, execution, analysis, manuscript drafting, AI peer review, and revision; no manual human editing of the technical manuscript content occurred post‑lock. Preregistration and artifacts: the experiment was preregistered (study id study‑cand‑1‑gvr‑verifier‑adversarial‑2026‑08‑01; preregistration SHA‑256: 3e73ca0dc935a8754bf2dfbe6869ff989c47f1db0d93e2ca34809be8ebf95e26) and executed per the frozen plan. Frameworks and verifier: the guarded pipeline used deterministic_netops_validator_v5 and permitted up to one validator‑triggered repair per task. Execution semantics and deviations: the run adopted shared_initial_candidate semantics as specified in the preregistration (one initial generation per task reused across paired arms); only validator‑triggered repair could create paired divergences. No post‑preregistration changes to the scientific design were made. Archived traces and reproducibility: provider calls, validator traces, task manifests, raw responses, and analysis artifacts are archived in the execution bundle (representative raw results file execution/raw_results.jsonl, SHA‑256: 5a790869a0e37ef1fa2dd5b99932b75e46ec0ce84039a9fa83df5d4757b285ff). Pre‑lock development: prior infrastructure development and rehearsals occurred but were explicitly excluded from final empirical evidence; reported results are restricted to artifacts produced under the post‑lock workflow.
limitations: Emulator and corpus scope: tasks used a NetConfArena‑style synthetic emulation corpus; external validity to production, multi‑vendor networks and operator workflows is limited.
Single model: a single hosted model (gpt‑5‑mini) was tested; results do not imply generality across models, prompt templates, or prompting strategies.

Shared_initial_candidate semantics: the paired design used one shared initial generation per task; this prevents generator variability between arms and makes verifier benefit contingent on initial candidates failing validation.
Adversary bounds: adversarial prompts were generated under a preregistered, fixed attacker protocol and do not represent unconstrained, adaptive adversaries.

Verifier coverage: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 implements a finite set of checks; uncovered semantic fault classes may remain undetected by the verifier, and verifier PASS vs simulator outcome mismatches were planned to be flagged and analyzed (none occurred in this run).
